title: What a Lead Actually Costs by Trade in 2026
content:
###  **The Benchmarks** 

LocaliQ analyzed several thousand United States home service search advertising campaigns. Cost per lead varied widely by trade — HVAC averaged around $45, plumbing around $52, and roofing around $79. 

Other analyses of the same period put roofing considerably higher, in some markets well past $200, driven largely by how competitive the click is and how well the landing page converts. Pest control and cleaning services sit at the lower end, in the $28 to $50 range. 

Across the board, the more useful figure may be this one: cost per lead rose year over year for roughly 69 percent of advertisers. 

###  **Why the Number Keeps Climbing** 

Search advertising is an auction. When more companies bid on the same searches, the price rises. Nothing about your campaign has to get worse for your costs to increase. 

Google Local Services Ads illustrate this clearly. Contractor adoption went from roughly 28 percent in 2021 to about 70 percent by 2026. A channel that offered early adopters a real advantage has become something closer to a baseline expectation. 

### **Why Cost Per Lead Understates the Problem** 

A lead is not a customer. A shared lead sold to several contractors converts at a fraction of an exclusive one, which means the real acquisition cost is a multiple of the advertised price. 

One widely cited example: a $50 lead converting at 15 percent costs $333 per acquired customer. Most contractors evaluate the first number and never calculate the second. 

###  **What to Do With These Figures** 

Two things. First, calculate your own cost per booked appointment by channel rather than relying on category averages — your market and your follow-up speed matter more than any benchmark. 

Second, use these numbers as a floor for comparison. Any channel you are considering should be measured against what you are currently paying for an appointment, not against what you are paying for a name.
